# Education in Sweden
Sweden’s education system is distinguished by its structure of free, publicly funded education from preschool (ages 1-6) through compulsory schooling (grundskola, nine years, ages 7-16) and into upper secondary school (gymnasieskola, three years, ages 16-19), which although elective, sees a 99% enrollment rate. Compulsory schooling covers a broad curriculum—Swedish, mathematics, English, sciences, arts, and social studies—with grades A-F starting in year 6. Upper secondary education offers 18 national programmes, divided between preparatory and vocational tracks, with students’ admission based on compulsory school grades. All programmes require completion of a diploma project and universal subjects. There are also introductory programs for students not meeting qualification criteria.
Higher education in Sweden is incorporated into the Bologna Process and divided into three levels: bachelor’s (180 credits), master’s (one or two years, 60/120 credits), and doctoral (PhD: four years, 240 credits; Licentiate: two years, 120 credits). Public universities and university colleges offer both general and professional degrees. Students are admitted based on upper secondary marks and standardized tests (SweSAT). Swedish and EU/EEA/Swiss citizens study tuition-free; others pay fees. Grading systems vary between institutions but align for European comparability. There is also a parallel publicly funded independent schools system (friskolor), which receives the same per-student funding as municipal schools and now enrolls a significant portion of students.
Sweden’s education system is regularly evaluated through international assessments such as PISA and PIRLS, with results sparking debate and ongoing reform efforts. The system is also notable for its anti-discrimination work, focus on inclusion (such as Sámi and special needs schools), and provision of extensive student financial aid.
